decisions.note: Role resolved, and it is a storage role rather than a signing one, which changes its priority. modules/sdk-core/src/bitgo/utils/opengpgUtils.ts wraps OpenPGP: it fetches BitGo's GPG public key (getBitgoGpgPubKey), encrypts and signs messages, and verifies share proofs over 'eddsa' | 'ecdsa' (verifyShareProof, verifySharedDataProof). That is how TSS key shares and their proofs are protected in transit and at rest, so harvest-now-decrypt-later applies: anything captured today is readable once a CRQC exists. The second anchor, bitgo/bip32util.ts, is BIP-32 key handling over @bitgo/secp256k1. Fixable today with a hybrid KEM around the share wrapping, independently of any signature migration.

Correct and specific enough to act on: modules/sdk-core/src/bitgo/trading/network/encrypt-rsa-browser.ts imports an SPKI PEM public key through WebCrypto with { name: 'RSA-OAEP', hash: 'SHA-256' } and usage ['encrypt'], deliberately reading window.crypto in the browser because crypto-browserify does not implement it. So this is RSA-OAEP key wrapping toward a server key in the trading network, and the ciphertext is transmitted and may be retained — harvest-now-decrypt-later, and the first candidate for a hybrid KEM because it is a client-to-server channel the vendor controls at both ends.

42 references across 14 files, and the file list is the point: besides the protocol (account-lib/mpc/tss/ecdsa/{ecdsa,types}.ts) it reaches bitgo/keychain/{iKeychains,keychains}.ts, i.e. the keychain representation. Paillier material that is persisted is a harvest-now-decrypt-later item, not only a future-signing one. As with the other two custodian libraries, this is the row a post-quantum signature standard does not fix: Paillier underpins the threshold protocol, NIST's 2024 standards are single-signer, and the multi-party threshold effort has not produced one.

The largest row here — 215 references across 16 files — spanning account-lib/mpc/util.ts, bitgo/baseCoin/iBaseCoin.ts, bitgo/keychain/keychains.ts, bitgo/pendingApproval/pendingApproval.ts and the tss modules. It is correct by the product's purpose, and the spread through pending approvals and base coin interfaces shows why a migration is not confined to a crypto module: the threshold scheme's identity is baked into the SDK's public types, so changing it is an API-compatibility exercise across every integrating customer.

modules/sdk-lib-mpc/src/tss/eddsa-mps/util.ts and redpallas-mps/util.ts — the multi-party signing helpers for EdDSA and for RedPallas, the Zcash Orchard signature scheme. Worth noting for its own sake: a custodian supporting Zcash shielded signing carries the same discrete-log exposure there as everywhere else, and Orchard's own post-quantum future is the subject of Shielded Labs' Epoch rather than of this SDK.

Two roles, both correct. Transaction and message signing: account-lib/baseCoin/secp256k1ExtendedKeyPair.ts, account-lib/util/crypto.ts, bitgo/ecdh.ts and bitgo/utils/tss/addressVerification.ts. Threshold signing and MPC: account-lib/mpc/curves/index.ts, account-lib/mpc/tss/ecdsa/ecdsa.ts and bitgo/utils/tss/ecdsa/{base,ecdsa}.ts. A CRQC derives the private key from a public key that is already on chain after the first spend, so for a custodian the exposure is proportional to how much of its address set has ever been spent from.
account-lib/baseCoin/ed25519KeyPair.ts and baseCoin/index.ts — transaction signing on the Ed25519 chains. Small row count, same migration class as the secp256k1 signing rows.

Accurate: across the three audited manifests (sdk-core, sdk-lib-mpc and the root package.json) the declared cryptography is @noble/curves, secp256k1 and tweetnacl, with nothing PQC-capable. In the JavaScript ecosystem, unlike on the Cortex-M targets in this portfolio, ML-KEM implementations are available (@noble/post-quantum among them), so for the key-wrapping rows above — OpenPGP share protection and the RSA-OAEP trading channel — a hybrid is a dependency choice today rather than a research problem. That makes this gap cheaper to close here than anywhere else in the custody slice, and it should be sequenced first.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — factoring
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Breaks RSA at every key length: a longer modulus only raises the cost polynomially. Plan migration to ML-KEM (or a hybrid) for key establishment and ML-DSA / SLH-DSA for signatures; start with keys protecting data that must stay confidential for years (harvest now, decrypt later) and with long-lived signatures.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Needs a fault-tolerant quantum computer. Published estimates for RSA-2048 fell from 20 million noisy qubits and 8 hours (Gidney–Ekerå 2021) to under a million noisy qubits and under a week (Gidney 2025); a 2026 neutral-atom design puts RSA-2048 one to two orders of magnitude slower than P-256 on 26,000 qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions; no such machine is publicly known.

quantum_algorithms.name: Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: 2026 estimates for a 256-bit curve: under 1,200 logical qubits and 90 million Toffoli gates, under half a million physical superconducting qubits running for minutes (Babbush et al.); 1,193 logical qubits with more gates (Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher); P-256 in a few days on 26,000 neutral-atom qubits (Cain et al.). Scenarios under stated assumptions, not forecasts.

quantum_algorithms.name: Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: The search is long and serial: NIST counts AES-128 key search as 2^170/MAXDEPTH quantum gates with MAXDEPTH between 2^40 and 2^96 and uses it as the yardstick of security category 1; a SHA-256 preimage was estimated at about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles on 2^12.6 logical qubits (Amy et al. 2016).

quantum_algorithms.name: Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim
quantum_algorithms.audit: 256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Bernstein (2009) argued that, once hardware cost is counted, it is not cheaper than classical parallel collision search; NIST defines security category 2 by SHA3-256 collision search counted in classical gates (2^146).

quantum_algorithms.name: Simon's algorithm — superposition attacks on symmetric constructions
quantum_algorithms.model_label: Q2: superposition queries to the victim's keyed primitive
quantum_algorithms.audit: No action for ordinary deployments of AES-GCM or CBC-MAC — the attack model does not apply. Record it as a model assumption; see the offline variant for Even–Mansour-type designs.
quantum_algorithms.practicality: Requires quantum access to the device that holds the key. A server encrypting classical messages does not give it; the model matters for quantum networks and some obfuscation settings.

scenario.rationale: Inside the 10-year horizon the survey puts at 28-49% ('quite possible'), and consistent with the BSI estimate of 15 years that 'could shrink to 10 or even less'. Use it for data that must stay confidential for decades, where being wrong is expensive.
